CHAPTER XXVIII. I AM SILENCED

I rubbed the water out of my eyes, and saw the raven on the edge of a
huge stone basin. With the cold light of the dawn reflected from his
glossy plumage, he stood calmly looking down upon me. I lay on my back
in water, above which, leaning on my elbows, I just lifted my face. I
was in the basin of the large fountain constructed by my father in the
middle of the lawn. High over me glimmered the thick, steel-shiny stalk,
shooting, with a torrent uprush, a hundred feet into the air, to spread
in a blossom of foam.

Nettled at the coolness of the raven’s remark,

“You told me nothing!” I said.

“I told you to do nothing any one you distrusted asked you!”

“Tut! how was mortal to remember that?”

“You will not forget the consequences of having forgotten it!” replied
Mr. Raven, who stood leaning over the margin of the basin, and stretched
his hand across to me.

I took it, and was immediately beside him on the lawn, dripping and
streaming.

“You must change your clothes at once!” he said. “A wetting does not
signify where you come from--though at present such an accident is
unusual; here it has its inconveniences!”

He was again a raven, walking, with something stately in his step,
toward the house, the door of which stood open.

“I have not much to change!” I laughed; for I had flung aside my robe to
climb the tree.

“It is a long time since I moulted a feather!” said the raven.

In the house no one seemed awake. I went to my room, found a
dressing-gown, and descended to the library.

As I entered, the librarian came from the closet. I threw myself on a
couch. Mr. Raven drew a chair to my side and sat down. For a minute or
two neither spoke. I was the first to break the silence.

“What does it all mean?” I said.

“A good question!” he rejoined: “nobody knows what anything is; a man
can learn only what a thing means! Whether he do, depends on the use he
is making of it.”

“I have made no use of anything yet!”

“Not much; but you know the fact, and that is something! Most people
take more than a lifetime to learn that they have learned nothing, and
done less! At least you have not been without the desire to be of use!”

“I did want to do something for the children--the precious Little Ones,
I mean.”

“I know you did--and started the wrong way!”

“I did not know the right way.”

“That is true also--but you are to blame that you did not.”

“I am ready to believe whatever you tell me--as soon as I understand
what it means.”

“Had you accepted our invitation, you would have known the right way.
When a man will not act where he is, he must go far to find his work.”

“Indeed I have gone far, and got nowhere, for I have not found my work!
I left the children to learn how to serve them, and have only learned
the danger they are in.”

“When you were with them, you were where you could help them: you left
your work to look for it! It takes a wise man to know when to go away; a
fool may learn to go back at once!”

“Do you mean, sir, I could have done something for the Little Ones by
staying with them?”

“Could you teach them anything by leaving them?”

“No; but how could I teach them? I did not know how to begin. Besides,
they were far ahead of me!”

“That is true. But you were not a rod to measure them with! Certainly,
if they knew what you know, not to say what you might have known, they
would be ahead of you--out of sight ahead! but you saw they were not
growing--or growing so slowly that they had not yet developed the
idea of growing! they were even afraid of growing!--You had never seen
children remain children!”

“But surely I had no power to make them grow!”

“You might have removed some of the hindrances to their growing!”

“What are they? I do not know them. I did think perhaps it was the want
of water!”

“Of course it is! they have none to cry with!”

“I would gladly have kept them from requiring any for that purpose!”

“No doubt you would--the aim of all stupid philanthropists! Why, Mr.
Vane, but for the weeping in it, your world would never have become
worth saving! You confess you thought it might be water they wanted: why
did not you dig them a well or two?”

“That never entered my mind!”

“Not when the sounds of the waters under the earth entered your ears?”

“I believe it did once. But I was afraid of the giants for them. That
was what made me bear so much from the brutes myself!”

“Indeed you almost taught the noble little creatures to be afraid of the
stupid Bags! While they fed and comforted and worshipped you, all the
time you submitted to be the slave of bestial men! You gave the darlings
a seeming coward for their hero! A worse wrong you could hardly have
done them. They gave you their hearts; you owed them your soul!--You
might by this time have made the Bags hewers of wood and drawers of
water to the Little Ones!”

“I fear what you say is true, Mr. Raven! But indeed I was afraid that
more knowledge might prove an injury to them--render them less innocent,
less lovely.”

“They had given you no reason to harbour such a fear!”

“Is not a little knowledge a dangerous thing?”

“That is one of the pet falsehoods of your world! Is man’s greatest
knowledge more than a little? or is it therefore dangerous? The fancy
that knowledge is in itself a great thing, would make any degree of
knowledge more dangerous than any amount of ignorance. To know all
things would not be greatness.”

“At least it was for love of them, not from cowardice that I served the
giants!”

“Granted. But you ought to have served the Little Ones, not the giants!
You ought to have given the Little Ones water; then they would soon
have taught the giants their true position. In the meantime you could
yourself have made the giants cut down two-thirds of their coarse
fruit-trees to give room to the little delicate ones! You lost your
chance with the Lovers, Mr. Vane! You speculated about them instead of
helping them!”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’
[Reference Rewrite]: “No room. Full up.”

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER II. INSIDE

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.
[Reference Rewrite]: I mapped the architecture of the isolated villa with the hyper-focused clarity that usually precedes hypothermic shock. An instant before, the torrential Victorian night had been a blur of freezing misery; now, my senses sharpened into jagged relief. The cold was a physical enemy, steadily liquefying the marrow in my bones and draining the last of my cellular energy. But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

generated_text:
I wiped the condensation from my optics, focusing on the silhouette perched atop the rim of the massive hydro-accumulator basin. Dawn's pale luminescence fractured against his iridescent feathers, casting a sharp, critical glare downward. I lay submerged in the coolant fluid, propped on my elbows, lifting my face just enough to register the threat.

I was positioned within the primary containment reservoir of the fountain system my progenitor had engineered centuries ago—a relic of hydraulic engineering situated in the center of the manicured lawn. Above me, the main injector shaft, a thick column of polished alloy, pierced the atmosphere, erupting a torrent of pressurized mist a hundred meters high before dissipating into a chaotic spray of droplets.

Stung by the avian entity's assessment—"You told me nothing!"—I retorted, my voice cracking slightly in the humid air. "I instructed you to ignore anyone you deemed untrustworthy!"

"Tut! How was a mortal mind expected to retain that directive?"

"You will not forget the cascading consequences of such negligence," Mr. Raven replied. The creature shifted, extending a clawed talon across the basin's edge. I grasped it, and instantly, the laws of physics bent to accommodate the transfer; I found myself standing on the grass, dripping wet, the sensation of gravity returning with a jolt.

"Immediate decontamination is required," he commanded, his tone devoid of malice but heavy with expectation. "Moisture accumulation is negligible in your origin sector, though here, in this controlled environment, it presents significant logistical complications."

He resumed his natural form, a raven of imposing stature, striding with deliberate precision toward the residence. Its entrance stood agape.

"I require minimal adjustment," I chuckled, stripping off my outer tunic to reveal the sleek, scaled integument beneath. "It has been an eternity since I shed a layer of armor."

"It is a long interval since you molted," the bird observed, pausing at the threshold.

Inside, the facility remained in a state of suspended animation. I proceeded to my quarters, donning a thermal regulation gown, and descended to the central archive. Upon entry, the custodian emerged from a storage alcove. I collapsed onto a reinforced sofa. Mr. Raven pulled a chair close, settling opposite me. Silence stretched between us, dense and heavy.

I broke the quiet first. "Explain the parameters of this situation."

"A pertinent inquiry," he responded. "Human cognition rarely grasps intrinsic meaning; it only interprets utility based on application. Whether understanding occurs depends entirely on how one leverages available data."

"I have applied no utility thus far."

"Scant progress, yes. Yet awareness of stagnation constitutes a baseline metric. Most species spend eons realizing they possess zero functional output. At minimum, you harbor the intent to contribute."

"My objective was to assist the Children—the Precious Little Ones."

"I acknowledge your motivation, yet your vector was flawed."

"I lacked the correct methodology."

"That is accurate, though culpability lies in your failure to seek it."

"I accept your premise, provided I comprehend the underlying mechanics."

"Acceptance of our summons would have aligned your trajectory. When an agent refuses action within their current locus, they must traverse vast distances to locate their function."

"I have traversed extensively and achieved null results. I failed to identify my function. I abandoned the Children to discover how to serve them, only to realize the magnitude of the peril threatening them."

"When co-located with them, you possessed the capacity to intervene. By departing to search for your role, you abdicated responsibility. Wisdom dictates knowing when to withdraw; folly compels immediate retreat."

"Do you imply I could have aided the Little Ones by remaining?"

"Did you attempt instruction by abandoning them?"

"No. However, what methodology existed? Furthermore, they surpassed my capabilities."

"That is factual. Yet you lacked the metric to gauge them. Had they possessed your knowledge—or potential insights—they would have eclipsed you exponentially. Instead, they exhibited stasis, or growth so imperceptible it suggested regression. They feared expansion. You have never witnessed a species capable of maintaining juvenile status indefinitely."

"But I possessed no agency to force maturation."

"You could have eliminated impediments to development."

"What obstacles? I identified none. I suspected perhaps a hydration deficit."

"Naturally. They lack the medium for vocalization."

"I would have prevented the necessity of such expression."

"Undoubtedly. The hallmark of incompetent altruism. Consider, Mr. Vane: were it not for the cacophony of distress, your civilization would never have warranted salvation. You hypothesized a water requirement; why did you not excavate aquifers?"

"That consideration never arose."

"Not even when subterranean acoustic signatures reached your sensors?"

"I recall a singular instance. However, I feared the Giants for their sake. That terror drove me to endure such abuse from the beasts myself!"

"In essence, you conditioned the noble offspring to dread the Stupid Bags. While they nourished, soothed, and revered you, you submitted to servitude under brutish overlords. You gifted the darlings a coward masquerading as a hero. A grievous error. They entrusted their hearts; you owe them your soul. You could have orchestrated the Giants into manual labor roles for the Little Ones."

"I concede the validity of your assertion, Mr. Raven. Yet I feared advanced knowledge might corrupt them, diminishing their innocence and aesthetic purity."

"They offered no justification for such apprehension."

"Is not limited knowledge inherently hazardous?"

"One of the foundational fallacies of your epoch. Does superior cognition render humanity greater, or does it introduce disproportionate risk? The notion that knowledge possesses inherent magnitude suggests any degree of enlightenment exceeds the danger of total ignorance. Omniscience is not greatness."

"At least my submission stemmed from affection, not timidity."

"Accepted. Nevertheless, you should have served the Little Ones, not the Giants. Providing them with water would have swiftly revealed the Giants' subordinate status. Simultaneously, you could have directed the Giants to prune two-thirds of their coarse flora to accommodate the delicate saplings. You squandered your opportunity with the Lovers, Mr. Vane. You engaged in speculation rather than execution."
